The English Reformation. Henry VIII's break with Rome and the Catholic Church, the English Reformation was undertaken primarily to secure an annulment for his marriage. Spanning the sixteenth century, it transformed England into a Protestant nation with the monarch as head of the Church of England, reshaping religious, political, and social life across the realm.

Henry VIII initiated the Reformation in the 1530s, chiefly to circumvent papal refusal to annul his marriage to Catherine of Aragon, daughter of Spanish monarchs, whose union had produced no male heir. Thomas Cromwell orchestrated the break from Rome and directed the suppression of monasteries, seizing their vast wealth for the Crown and enriching both himself and the nobility.

Henry introduced the Act of Supremacy in 1534, declaring the monarch, not the Pope, as supreme head of the Church of England, a radical assertion of royal authority over spiritual matters. The monasteries were dissolved between 1536 and 1541, destroying centuries of religious institutions and redirecting land and resources to the nobility, fundamentally reshaping English landholding patterns. Through the Church of England Act of 1534, Henry established a national church nominally Catholic in doctrine but Protestant in governance.

The Latin Mass was replaced with an English-language Book of Common Prayer, first introduced in 1549, making worship accessible to ordinary people and advancing English as a liturgical language. Henry's personal religious views remained ambiguous: he rejected papal authority but maintained Catholic doctrine on several sacraments, calling himself "Defender of the Faith." The Reformation's religious character shifted under his Tudor heirs. Edward VI pushed more radical Protestantism, Mary I briefly restored Catholicism and persecuted Protestants, and Elizabeth I established a moderate middle way.

The English Reformation resulted in significant loss of life. Thomas More and John Fisher were executed for refusing the oath of supremacy, symbolizing the spiritual struggle over royal authority. The Reformation established the Church of England as distinct from both Rome and continental Protestantism, laying the foundation for Anglicanism and creating a unique church structure blending Catholic hierarchy with Protestant theology.
